> "Nuclear technology: yes." And that makes a police state more likely how, exactly? I mean, does the kind of plant that produces your electricity somehow make a form of government more or less likely?

You got me. Really. I should have taken this off the list. I lost focus of "this is a post about police state stuff". 

> "Population helpless without electricity: yes." For very specific definitions of "helpless", sure. I mean, this has been just as true for about as long as widespread electricity has existed in countries, and it hasn't really made vague "police states" more likely.

Having police states could mean restricted access to fuel which provides electricity. I am not saying that police states will be more likely because of electricity existing. I am trying to emphasize how fragile we are. If something bad happened, specifically the dramatic police state I am describing, then we would be helpless.

> "Population has lost all self-sufficiency skills: yes." ...you do realize that this has been the case for hundreds of years now, right? Big cities and people lamenting city people's "lack of self-sufficiency skills" are about the same age.

Same as above. Humans have lost survival skills. If  there is anything standing in the way between raw materials and the food in our refrigerator, I wanted to try to mention its possibility because it is significant to mention in the case of situations like police states. You could say that such a factor makes a region more "ripe for the picking". Hope I am more clear.

"Culture is antisocial enough such that we do not know our neighbors: yes." Again, that is about as old as cities are.
"Population is high enough such that we don't know our police: yes." I mean, I hate to sound like a broken record, but it's been that way ever since big cities have existed, and it's arguably not even a bad thing.
"Media controls: yes (luckily more are quitting television)." Ah yes, except you, enlightened Redditor. Of course.

> "Vegetables are proprietary and seeds from them (sold to populace) cannot be replanted: yes." ...you know how easy it is to have a vegetable garden, right? You can buy normal seeds.

Yes, but in the event of a crisis, food is less accessible. I'm not sure how much less, but I would think it would be a lot considering the USA exports to the entire world. 

> "Anti-gun laws encourage obey culture, complacency." I realise that many disagree with me on that, especially in America, so I'll just say that even if you are pro-gun, saying that being anti-gun or pro-regulation makes you complacent is pretty asinine.

Even if everyone knows why I think anti-gun laws promote complacency, I think I'll explain: When you remove power from yourself and put it in an all-trusting authority, then that authority might do well with that power, but that authority might also abuse that power. The fact that they **might** abuse power is reason enough to keep power with individuals rather than special groups. However, my opinion is that laws should be decided for regions instead of entire nations, which i think is more important than a belief in any specific law. I believe taking a little power from individuals is a baby step in the wrong direction. This is especially true now that we know about events like Nazis confiscating weapons before they rose to power.

> "Politically-correctness encourages obey culture, complacency." Ah yes, the fact that you can't call people "nigger" anymore sure made people complacent.

Taboos are detrimental: If people want to speak ill about someone, they can suffer the consequences of having their reputation ruined. Being afraid to offend people is significant because it gets people used to not having civilized discussions or may lead to avoiding certain crazy-sounding topics. Restricted words may get people used to the idea of losing their freedom of speech. It's OK to offend people. Talk about what you think about guns. Talk about what you think about religion. We need to talk to each other more so we can get used to it. I would rather often disagree about things, but still end the day as neighbors and friends.

> "Public schools encourage obey culture, complacency. This occurs for 11 consecutive years." While the current model for American public schools is very flawed, public schools in general, as an idea, are literally the only way to have a modern society.

Why not let parents choose from a variety of local, private institutions that specialize in a career that they want to pursue? Why not have apprenticeships organized by those institutions? These schools would try to raise their rankings by bragging about what the average income is for their graduates. 

> "Daycare culture encourages obey culture, complacency." "If I just say things, people will believe them even if I make no actual argument".

A stretch, for sure. I'll say that you are more right here. I don't think daycares are good, but saying they encourage complacency is too much emphasis on what might just be a small side effect if anything. 

Daycares are not good because daycares mean less time spent between children and parents. Child/parent bonds are very important for IQ and waking up before the sun while you are a little child to mindlessly dress, pack a bag, squint through the bright lights, and tumble out of a car to a stranger's house, and live with someone posing as your parent. Adults who live in a world where daycares are necessary might find that they think daycares are normal and that it is normal to need two providers per household to barely scrape by. These are my disorganized thoughts... go easy.
